name: Tara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is lectures on structures and surveying, then evenings copying my notes out neatly by hand, because that's how things stick for me. I work Saturday and Sunday on the checkout at a supermarket on the ring road. I live in a flat with two other first-years, and my parents pay the rent and I pay for food and bus passes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can point at a bridge and say you helped it stand up. My dad is a plumber and I used to go on site visits with him and look at the drawings. My results were average, so I wasn't sure I'd get in, and I still check my timetable three times a day in case I've got it wrong. I don't use any AI tools. I like knowing why an answer is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. At the checkout we already have self-service tills and they mostly make queues, so I'd say the hype is silly. I'd keep my opinion to myself online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved but not carefree. Money is still tight when my parents pay rent and I'm covering the rest. A bridge needs engineers whatever happens, so I'd expect to find work in four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now. Keep both supermarket shifts, keep copying my notes, keep going to the study group on Tuesdays. I'd try to get a site visit placement with a local firm, since the department told us those fill up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough, though never fully, because I'm a worrier by nature. I always imagine the thing going wrong before it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about when things stay normal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and exams. The supermarket might cut weekend hours, since they've already brought in more self-service tills. If they did, I'd be down about sixty pounds a week, and that's my food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the hours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my mum if I could eat at home more often, and I'd look for a Saturday job at a garden centre. I'd hate to tell my parents I'm struggling, because they already pay a lot.

say: I'd say I **expected** it, since the self-service tills at work mostly make queues.
I'd keep my opinion off social media.
think: A bridge needs **engineers** whatever happens, so I should find work in four years.
Money is still tight, with my parents paying rent.
do: Keep both supermarket **shifts** and the Tuesday study group.
Apply for a site placement with a local firm before places fill up.
feel: I feel **calm** enough, but I'm a worrier and imagine things going wrong first.
S0.quote: I'd hate to tell my parents I'm struggling, because they already pay a lot.
fieldNote: Her worry is **weekend hours** at the checkout, where self-service tills are already cutting shifts.
Resistant style: sticks to routines, copies notes by hand, no AI.
Would hide money trouble from her parents.

steps.text: Keep both weekend shifts on the supermarket checkout
Apply for a site visit placement with a local engineering firm
Look for a garden centre Saturday job if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see how it goes, since nothing's proven yet. At work I'd say the checkout is already half machines. I wouldn't post online, because I don't know enough to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it frightens me a bit. The drawing and checking part of engineering is what they say AI is good at, and I don't use any of it, so I'd fall behind. I'd tell myself that site work and safety still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to learn at least the engineering software they actually use, like the design packages the lecturers show us. I'd ask my dad's firm if I could watch how the estimating works. I'd stay away from chatbots still, but I'd allow myself to see one used by someone I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like someone changed the rules of the game while I was getting good at the old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch someone you trust use one. Who would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lecturer in structures, Dr Hale, who seems fair. He doesn't push it, and he says check everything. If a person like that says it's safe for homework, I'd try it for a week, no more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop doing to make time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably one of the weekend shifts, which would hurt the budget. I'd rather do that than fall behind in my course. A degree is the thing I'm paying for with my whole life.

say: I'd say let's **wait** and see, since nothing is proven yet.
At work I'd say the checkout is already half machines.
think: Drawing and checking are what AI is good at, and I've never used it, so I might fall **behind**.
Site work and safety still need people.
do: Learn the engineering **software** lecturers show us and ask my dad's firm about estimating.
Watch a trusted lecturer use an AI tool before trying it for a week.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, as if the rules changed while I was getting good at the old ones.
S1.quote: A degree is the thing I'm paying for with my whole life.
fieldNote: She admits **fear** of falling behind because she has avoided AI.
Will trust a lecturer, not the internet, before trying a tool.
Would drop a weekend shift for study, which hurts her budget.

steps.text: Learn the design software lecturers use in structures labs
Ask her dad's firm to show how estimating works
Try one AI tool for a week with her lecturer's guidance
Drop one weekend shift to protect study time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say. I'd probably tell my parents first and leave the internet out of it. At work, I'd see the tills and feel a bit sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my whole plan collapsed. Two years and thinking AI can do the design work, and I'm in the middle of my degree with nothing to show. Robots on site come around 2031, so site work might last longer, but plumbing and building are the next to go after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about the plumbing trade, since there's no time to wait. I'd cut my spending to the bare minimum and keep the checkout shifts for as long as they exist. And I'd ask the university whether anyone is giving advice, since I don't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd feel sick and I probably wouldn't sleep well for weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would be hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not knowing which thing to do first. I'm a person who needs a plan, and a plan needs time. I'd freeze for a month, and then my dad would say get up and get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say a good plumber will always have work, and then he'd go quiet, because he knows robots could do it in ten years. He'd try to make me feel better and I'd see he was worried too.

say: I'd tell my **parents** first and keep it off the internet.
At work I'd look at the tills and feel a bit sick.
think: My whole plan has **collapsed**, with thinking AI doing design work before I graduate.
Site work lasts longer, but plumbing and building are next after about 2031.
do: Talk to my dad about the **plumbing** trade, since there's no time to wait.
Cut spending to the bare minimum and ask the university for advice.
feel: I feel **frightened** and wouldn't sleep well for weeks.
S2.quote: I'm a person who needs a plan, and a plan needs time.
fieldNote: Her need for **planning** meets a two-year deadline; she expects to freeze for a month.
Looks to her father and the plumbing trade as a fallback, but sees its limits.
Seeks outside advice because she doesn't know where to start.

steps.text: Ask her dad whether she could train as a plumber
Cut spending to rent share, food and bus pass only
Book an appointment with the university careers advice service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still scary, but I can work with it. I'd talk it over with my parents and my study group. I'd probably say we should get proper advice from the university, not guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, and the design work would be going just as I start. That's bad timing. But I'd have a few years to make a real place for myself, with contacts, a licence and site experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get placements in each summer, aim for professional registration, and try to land a job at a firm that does site work, since that lasts longer. I'd learn at least one design tool. And I'd keep both shifts and save what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan, which makes it easier to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can take things one at a time. With two years I'd be running, but with five I can study properly and still do something about it. It's the difference between a flood and a rising river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most concerned about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, who's a dental receptionist. Booking and answering the phone are exactly what the AI does. I'd tell her to learn the clinic's software, and to start looking for a clinical role.

say: I'd say it's scary but I can **work** with five years.
I'd ask the university for proper advice instead of guessing.
think: Graduating in 2029 means design work is going just as I start, so **timing** is bad.
I'd still have time to build contacts and site experience.
do: Get a summer **placement** every year and aim for professional registration.
Learn one design tool and keep both shifts, saving what I can.
feel: I feel **worried** but with a plan, which is easier to carry.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be running, but with five I can study properly and still do something about it.
fieldNote: Five years gives her the **plan** she needs and lowers the panic.
Worries about her mum, a dental receptionist whose tasks are thinking tasks.
Still sees the design work disappearing as she graduates.

steps.text: Get a summer site placement in each of the next three years
Learn one design package properly in year two
Save a little from each supermarket wage towards a cushion
Tell her mum to learn the clinic's software and look at clinical roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a decade is enough, and we should all be sensible. I'd say we should teach people about it in schools. I'd probably still not use it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 28 in 2036. That's plenty of time to qualify, work on a few projects and see how things go. I'd think engineers who can be on site will be fine for a long while, since robots come three years after the thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a job with a firm that does bridges or water works, and save for a deposit. I'd take one course a year in new software. I'd also learn a language or two, as a plan B, in case I want to work abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not happy, but okay. I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you still wouldn't use it much. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like knowing how my answer was built. But I'd realise at some point that other people are faster than me, and then I'd have to give in. I'd try it slowly, on small jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody knows whether ten years means ten years. I'd not take on too much debt. Keeping a bit of money aside is like carrying an umbrella on a day that's probably dry.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough and schools should teach people about it.
I'd probably still not use it much myself.
think: I'd be 28 in 2036, with plenty of time to **qualify** and see how things go.
Engineers on site should be fine for a long while.
do: Finish the degree, join a firm doing **bridges** or water works, and save for a deposit.
Take one software course a year and learn a language as plan B.
feel: I feel **okay**, not happy, and at least I can breathe.
S4.quote: Keeping a bit of money aside is like carrying an umbrella on a day that's probably dry.
fieldNote: A decade eases her **planning** panic, but she keeps a money cushion.
She expects to give in to AI tools eventually and try them slowly on small jobs.
Her caution is a trait, not just a reaction.

steps.text: Take a job with a firm that builds bridges or water works
Keep a small amount aside each month as a safety cushion
Try one AI tool on small coursework tasks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. A plan needs time and two years doesn't give any. What would help is clear advice from the university, some warning from government, and firms that keep taking on trainees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more flexible than I look. I'm slow to change, but when I've decided, I stick to it. I just need someone to tell me the truth about what's coming, in plain words.

headlineQuote: I'm slow to change, but when I've decided, I stick to it.
portrait: Tara is an **18-year-old** civil engineering student who works weekends at a supermarket checkout and copies her notes by hand.
She sits in the political centre, avoids AI tools and leans on her **plumber** dad for advice.
She needs a plan, so a short warning shakes her badly and a long one lets her breathe.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** at plateau to alarmed at two years, then back to anxious and uneasy.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because she needs time to plan and wouldn't know what to do first.
whatWouldHelp: Plain **advice** from the university, warning from government and firms that keep taking trainees.
